Title:
Euclidean embedding of discrete-time Markov chains for anomaly detection

Authors:
Abhishek Gupta, Srinivas Aluru, and Suman Banerjee

Abstract:
We propose a new method for detecting anomalies in discrete-time Markov chains (MCs) on finite state spaces using a Euclidean embedding of the Kullback-Leibler divergence. Our approach calculates upper and lower bounds for the anomaly score, validated empirically. The method is entirely computational, requiring no human input, and excels particularly in detecting rare anomalies. Designed for unsupervised, i.e., domain-agnostic, application, the paper provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the approach. Empirical studies demonstrate the method's performance and its potential advantages. We provide a complete implementation of the method and a repository of synthetic datasets. Additionally, we present code for verifying the theoretical claims of our work.

remains a significant challenge in database privacy. This study introduces a novel approach to enhancing utility while maintaining privacy. Our method involves relaxing the constraints of existing frameworks through three key strategies. First, we apply a transformation to the private domain of the database using clustering techniques, thereby reducing the range of sensitive values and improving the efficiency of privacy-preserving methods. Second, we derive a new analytical formula for the lower bound of information leakage, enabling the optimization of parameters within frameworks like k-anonymity and l-diversity to minimize leaked information. We conducted 3D hydrodynamic simulations incorporating radiative transfer, utilizing an analytic radiative transfer code to determine ionization rates and ion numbers throughout the disk. These rates are essential for a radiatively photoevaporative model. Our findings indicate that X-ray photoevaporation can generate gas substructures, whereas FUV photoevaporation is unlikely to do so. Additionally, the gas surface density resulting from X-ray photoevaporation aligns well with the dust surface density in the TW Hya system. Future research will explore the impact of additional factors, such as dust grain growth and gas cooling, on substructure formation. Given that DUSTPIPER disk models suggest many systems have dust surface densities comparable to TW Hya, X-ray photoevaporation may be a prevalent mechanism for creating emission substructures. Furthermore, the presence of ionization peaks generated by both X-rays and FUV radiation offers a method to estimate the relative contributions of these radiation types in ionized gas. Finally, we anticipate that the interplay between X-ray and FUV photoevaporation will significantly influence the morphology of photoevaporative cavities.

When the raft is confined to a single-dimensional line and the density of R molecules is low, a phase transition from liquid to solid occurs as the system is stretched. Finally, the work provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for predicting the mechanical properties of these active systems. While retrieving relevant facts can guide answers to query-specific queries (SEQA), general knowledge questions often require a search engine to retrieve information from open sources. This study investigates whether it is feasible to guide retrieval for open-domain question answering without training on annotated data. We utilize search results from a search engine to knowledge-based QA and employ transfer learning to evaluate the necessity of label data for QA models. Our experiments address two primary inquiries: 1) Can we enhance QA performance using search results when only unlabelled data is available? 2) Does label data enhance performance by enabling the model to more effectively align with the task? We compare various models and information retrieval techniques using both weak and strong retrieval methods. Our findings indicate that it is possible to improve performance using search results in the absence of label data. However, QA models equipped with relevant search results struggle to filter out noise from results that do not align with the question. Consequently, we observe that it is generally impossible to significantly boost performance in this context. Furthermore, we find that it is crucial to train models with label data to ensure they can effectively focus on retrieved results. Finally, it is important to note that while it is difficult to improve performance using search results in the absence of label data, it is generally impossible to do so using results even when label data is available. This is because models trained with label data fail to leverage search results when dealing with questions they do not know. These results underscore the inherent challenges in knowledge-based QA and highlight the need for further research in this area. This paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.00827.

This study introduces a novel method for localizing the source of incident nonrelativistic MW electrons by analyzing the amplitude and phase patterns of terahertz (THz) radiation generated when these electrons strike a metal surface. A analytical model is developed to reveal the underlying mechanism of electron-induced THz emission, which is then validated through a comprehensive numerical analysis covering a broad spectrum of electron and source parameters. This research demonstrates that the THz signal's amplitude and phase are highly sensitive to the source's longitudinal and angular positions. Consequently, a new technique is established that enables the precise determination of the source parameters with exceptional accuracy. Finally, the practical applicability of this approach is confirmed by examining the characteristics of electron and source beams from various sources. The findings indicate that this method holds significant potential for use in electron diffraction, scattering, and imaging studies. Furthermore, it offers fundamental insights into how electron beams interact with matter at the nanoscale. In light of these results, the proposed technique is anticipated to be valuable for advancing both practical applications and fundamental science. Additionally, this work lays the foundation for a new class of instruments known as electron beam tomographs, which operate on a principle analogous to x-ray tomography. In this context, the incident nonrelativistic electron beam functions as the x-ray beam, while a time-resolved THz detector serves as the x-ray sensor. By extending the well-known tomography reconstruction algorithms to the time domain, the electron beam's three-dimensional distribution can be reconstructed from time-resolved THz measurements taken along multiple projections. This methodology represents a new era in tomography, where the electron beam is utilized as a tomographic light source. Such a development could facilitate the investigation of charge and energy propagation within nano- and micro-objects, thereby enabling the next generation of tomographic imaging techniques. Moreover, this approach could aid in the search for new sources of MW electrons. Specifically, it enables the measurement of the full parameter set of electron beams emitted by various new sources, including cold cathodes, field emitters, nanotips, nano- and micro-objects, and nanoantennas. This capability is essential for the accurate characterization of electron beam properties, a prerequisite for the widespread application of electron beams in areas such as medicine, agriculture, and security. Furthermore, the technique is directly applicable to the emerging field of MW electron beam tomography, which holds promise for diagnosing and monitoring various physical, biological, and chemical processes.

This introduction outlines the core principles of this approach and provides an overview of the papers included in the issue. Additionally, an invitation for a special issue on modeling shared human-world understanding is extended. Finally, the subsequent sections detail the process of selecting the included papers and explain the motivation behind this specific focus. Special issues often arise from particular interests or gaps in current research; however, this case differs. The decision to create this issue stems from the belief that defining a specific concept of intelligence is more valuable than merely addressing individual problems in isolation. Consequently, this issue seeks to elucidate and promote a distinct vision of intelligence. This introduction concludes by summarizing the contributions of each section.

This paper proposes a novel method for detecting anomalous events using a generative auto-encoder. Specifically, we employ a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) to encode video sequences, subsequently identifying anom Events by analyzing the reconstruction error of these sequences. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, we address a critical challenge in existing research regarding the scarcity of training data for anomaly detection. To mitigate this, we propose training the VAE on a dataset that encompasses not only anomalous events but also a broader range of activities. We evaluate our method on two public datasets: UCF-101 Extended and JODI. On the JODI dataset, our results surpass those of current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we conducted extensive experiments on the UCf-101 Extended dataset to demonstrate the robustness of our approach. To our knowledge, no prior studies have utilized a VAE for anomaly detection on this dataset. Our findings indicate that our method effectively identifies diverse anomalous events, including those that do not align with the typical characteristics of the event categories. Finally, to enhance interpretability, we provide qualitative results and analysis.

This approach enables scaling graph analytics to massive datasets by replacing graphs with high-dimensional vectors, thereby supporting various machine learning workflows. Although widely adopted, this method introduces a risk of data leakage during the vectorization step. Specifically, when node labels are used in embeddings like those generated by label propagation algorithms, the resulting vectors encode both topological and categorical data. This violates the fundamental assumption that node vectors should exclusively represent graph topology, leading to biased analyses. To solve this data leakage problem, we propose a privacy-aware embedding framework that utilizes graph cut techniques to create masked node embeddings. These vectors retain only the necessary topological details for specific graph analyses while omitting any leaked information. We validate our framework's efficacy through experiments on real-world graph classification and semi-supervised classification tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in preventing data leakage. In this study, we extend the framework of vector measures with values in a locally convex space E, introducing $\tau$-measures and $\tau$-continuity relative to a given countable family of subsets of the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of a topological space X. We establish a Riesz-type theorem that characterizes these $\tau$-measures using regular measures of continuity, specifically within the context of Hausdorff locally convex spaces. As a consequence, we derive a Dixmier-type theorem for such spaces, demonstrating that any continuous linear functional on E* which is weakly *-representable by an E-measure can be approximated in the vague topology of E'* by measures that are both positive and of countable variation. Additional properties and applications of these $\tau$-measures are explored and presented. Finally, we establish a Krein-Milman-type theorem concerning the compact convex hull of the images of positive $\tau$-measures, which generalizes the classical Krein-Milman theorem to broader classes of locally convex spaces.

This study identifies these necessary conditions for compact objects by analyzing light deflection, gravitational redshift, and the conditions for mass gain via photon absorption. analyze the stability of kink and antikink solutions within the $\phi^6$-type field theory in both $(1+1)$ and $(1+3)$ dimensions. Using a perturbation approach, the stability of kink solutions under small perturbations transverse to the knot is evaluated. The analytical findings indicate that while anti-kinks are inherently stable, kinks possess a finite lifetime before decaying. Furthermore, numerical solutions derived via the pseudo-spectral method confirm these predictions. Specifically, in $(1+1)$ dimensions, the decay time of kinks is observed to be proportional to the initial transverse perturbation amplitude. Conversely, in $(1+3)$ dimensions, the initial slope of the energy versus time graph for both kinks and anti-kinks is directly proportional to the square of the initial perturbation amplitude. Additionally, the numerical results demonstrate that the transverse component of the energy exhibits a positive sign for kinks and a negative sign for anti-kinks during the early stages of evolution. Finally, the model's ability to support both anti-kinks and stable (or metastable) kinks serves as a distinguishing feature compared to many other models. Finally, this paper introduces a comprehensive review of the various analytical and numerical techniques utilized to assess the stability of topological solitons. These ultra-short pulses are created through high-order harmonic generation, resulting in a spectro-temporal coupling that necessitates deconvolution to precisely determine the temporal characteristics of the pulse. This study introduces a novel measurement technique that eliminates this coupling, thereby directly yielding the attosecond pulse duration. Additionally, the technique could facilitate the measurement of the natural lifetime of valence autoionizing resonances. The proposed measurement protocol utilizes a standard RABITA (Recombination of Atoms by Interference of Two-Color Above-threshold Ionization) interferometer, relying on the maximum-likelihood estimation of the ion yield's global maximum. This is achieved by employing a strong He I 2p resonance ionization laser and a highly sensitive electron energy analyzer. This formulation demonstrates that the FWHM remains independent of the pulse train's repetition rate and the electron energy spectrometer's resolution, provided the spectrometer's point spread function is symmetric. Finally, a simplified expression for the attosecond pulse duration is proposed for scenarios involving small relative ion yield fluctuations. Under these conditions, the attosecond pulse duration can be directly measured from the full width at half maximum of the ionization signal, with the uncertainty determined by electron energy spectrometer noise. This study analyzes the Cargo ecosystem using publicly available data, examining its composition, evolution, and structure through the lenses of applications, packages, and networks of package dependencies and versions. The research identifies key metrics for evaluating ecosystem health, including the distribution of package usage, the distribution of package maintenance responsibilities, and the level of maintenance redundancy. Finally, the study reveals that maintainers often focus on a small number of packages, while a large group of packages receives no maintenance. These results have significant implications for understanding ecosystem structure and for tools aimed at improving package maintenance. Ultimately, the analysis underscores the need for ecosystems to encourage maintainers to take on new packages and to foster maintenance among a diverse range of packages.

While ground-based radial velocity surveys have confirmed many such planets around massive stars, their significant stellar activity introduces noise that hinders the detection of small planets. This study demonstrates that machine learning can effectively model this activity-induced noise using high-cadence photometry and light curves. We developed a custom convolutional neural network (CNN) designed to estimate stochastic activity noise suitable for exoplanet detection. By training the model on high-quality Kepler data, we show it surpasses traditional Gaussian process methods in predicting synthetic planet signals within noisy environments. Furthermore, we applied this machine learning approach to validate confirmed exoplanets, analyzing a large sample of over 1,000 radial velocity candidates with known rotation periods. Our results indicate that the model successfully recovers planet signals for nearly all targets where a planet is present, while accurately modeling the stellar variability of non-planet hosts. These findings suggest that machine learning offers a promising avenue for characterizing exoplanets around rapidly rotating, active stars. This work represents the first demonstration of a CNN applied to exoplanet noise modeling and marks a significant advancement in the field. A Python package, AstroML-LMGP, is available to replicate these results. Our analysis of radial velocity data reveals that a CNN can precisely model stellar activity in over 90% of the targets, making it a powerful tool for identifying and validating exoplanets around highly active stars. Ultimately, this technique will be essential for confirming Earth-mass planets around active stars and for re-analyzing existing radial velocity datasets. A robust implementation of this method could significantly enhance the current exoplanet catalog. Additionally, we have made a Gaussian process model of stellar activity, trained on Kepler data, available as an open-source Gaussian process library within the AstroML-LMGP package. This resource allows researchers to gauge the level of stellar activity noise in their data and assess its impact on planet detection and parameter estimation. The code is accessible at https://github.com/AstroML/AstroML-LMGP. as a dominant force in machine learning, driving significant advancements across numerous fields. However, their extensive parameter counts and layered architectures often result in models that are computationally and energetically inefficient for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Quantization offers an effective solution to these challenges by substituting low-precision fixed-point numbers for the high-precision weights and activations typical of modern DNNs. Despite this efficiency, existing quantization techniques frequently compromise model accuracy. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the semantic information embedded within models to guide the adaptation of per-channel quantization parameters. Specifically, we employ a graph attention network to compute attention scores for each node within the DNN architecture, utilizing these scores to determine per-channel scaling factors for fixed-point weights and quantization parameters for activations. This methodology enables us to identify scaling factors that maintain the structural and functional integrity of the original high-precision model. Our approach, implemented as a PyTorch plugin, is compatible with various state-of-the-art frameworks. Empirical results on both ImageNet and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing solutions, achieving accuracy levels comparable to unquantized models. Furthermore, our technique outperforms other high-precision compression methods in terms of accuracy, size, and speed. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through statistical analysis of activation value distributions and the impact of semantic data on quantization. The implementation can be accessed at: https://github.com/AlirezaShahbazian/SKAQ. Source code for reproducibility is also available at the same repository. Index Terms--Deep Neural Networks, Quantization, Fixed-Point Arithmetic, Graph Attention Networks, Semantic Information.

In this paper, we establish a general framework for analyzing the asymptotic behavior of random matrices composed of a finite number of independent random matrices. This approach enables the computation of the limiting spectral distribution for polynomials and formal power series in these matrices. As applications, we determine the asymptotic eigenvalue distributions for random circulant and Hankel matrices. Additionally, we examine random symmetric matrices formed as sums of products of independent random matrices and their transposes. We also evaluate and contrast this methodology with alternative techniques, including those based on directed graphs and noncrossing partitions, as well as representations via free multiplicative functions. Finally, we discuss extensions of these findings to random matrices over finite fields and rings.

Building on the framework introduced in [17], which links the asymptotics of random matrices to the analytic properties of random analytic functions, this study examines random power series defined by nonlinear compositions. We derive general formulas for the $n$-th moments of these series and apply these results to analyze the asymptotics of random polynomials and power series arising from Cayley graphs of finitely generated groups. Specifically, we establish conditions under which the eigenvalue distribution of random polynomials in free random variables converges to a limit distribution supported on a smooth curve. We illustrate this with examples involving products of independent random matrices and their transposes, and directed graphs on $\mathbb{Z}^d$. Moreover, we present a novel approach to determining the zero sets of random polynomials and apply this to analyze the eigenvalues of random polynomials in symmetric random matrices.

Although hardware-in-the-loop testing can expose vulnerabilities, it is often impractical for systems that hybridize real hardware with simulated components. This article introduces FuzzedHardware-in-the-Loop (FHL), a framework enabling comprehensive, targeted, and randomized testing of interfaces between physical devices and their simulated environments. FuzzedFHL augments the capabilities of traditional hardware-in-the-loop setups by facilitating attacks on both simulated systems and interaction points between HIL components. It supports three distinct testing strategies: complete, targeted, and randomized. The framework integrates complete and targeted FHL approaches to develop a novel technique for generating multi-step, chained attacks on interactions between HIL elements. Furthermore, FuzzedFHL implements these attacks within a closed-loop system using an evolutionary strategy to maximize, maintain, and explore the test coverage of a specified objective function. To validate the framework's efficacy, we present two case studies: first, applying it to a common control engineering challenge of stabilizing an inverted pendulum on a cart, and second, demonstrating its utility in probing the decision-making processes of machine learning models. In the first case study, FuzzedFHL successfully identified physical system failures that comprehensive hardware testing missed. In the second, it achieved a significantly higher exploration rate (100% vs. 10%) and discovered failure modes that other methods failed to detect. These findings indicate that FuzzedFHL can substantially broaden the scope of hardware-in-the-loop testing, making it ideal for hardening physical systems against subtle, otherwise undetectable attacks. The FuzzedFHL framework is accessible at https://github.com/CSSE-ETH/FuzzedFHL.

This paper introduces infinite q-series that encompass these apéry-type binomial series as special cases, with the latter emerging when $q$ approaches 1. 3429.08-002032.0, a candidate variable source potentially exhibiting Type IIa optical light curves, revealed a significant flux increase between 2018 and 2019 across all infrared bands. This variation was notably distinct from the source's fainter pre-2018 state. Between May 2018 and May 2019, the source brightened by approximately 1.5 magnitudes in the WISE $W1$ and $W2$ bands, with the latter showing a slope consistent with steady reprocessing of accretion disk light by a circumstellar dust shell. However, the $W1$ light curve deviates from this linear trend at both temporal extremes, a pattern inconsistent with standard dwarf nova models. Given the source's proximity to the Galactic plane, interstellar extinction may influence these light curves, though this hypothesis remains unconfirmed. The source's position within the dwarf nova instability strip suggests it is a cataclysmic variable; nevertheless, its unusual properties and light curves indicate a novel outburst event. Consequently, this case represents a compelling outlier that warrants further investigation into the physics of accretion in cataclysmic variables. If similar objects exist, they could offer critical insights into the diverse outburst behaviors observed in this class of variable. This outlier status is further highlighted by the absence of known near-infrared light curves for any previously identified dwarf nova. We recommend that future infrared surveys of cataclysmic variables prioritize monitoring known unstable systems to identify additional instances of this phenomenon. Such a approach would facilitate the classification of this unusual object and enable a statistical analysis of these rare events. Additionally, the source's instability is evidenced by a low mass transfer rate of $\dot{M} \approx 10^{-9} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$, derived from the outburst luminosity and an equilibrium blackbody temperature of $T_{eq} \approx 1000 K$. This rate aligns with the lower boundary of values typically associated with dwarf nova outbursts. Finally, we note that the source is not a known Tidal Disruption Event, as it lacks the characteristic blue optical light curve and near-infrared light curve slope associated with such phenomena.

the growth of liquid metal droplets on substrates. This study investigates how these conditions influence droplet dynamics through simulations of a super-droplet collection process. A substrate located at $z=0$ attracts droplets rising from $z=h$ along vertical lines, resulting in a collection efficiency $\eta$ that varies with the dimensionless distance $h/R$. Our results show that $\eta$ is highly sensitive to boundary conditions, particularly solid shear stress $\tau_s$ and liquid slip length $b$. Specifically, when solid shear stress is significant and slip is low, $\eta$ surpasses 0.9 for distances $h/R \geq 10$. We also propose a universal scaling for $\eta$ as a function of the Péclet number Pe and the above parameters, which aligns with existing literature and extends its scope. Finally, this scaling is employed to determine the critical Péclet number for an infinite collection efficiency, yielding $\eta_{crit} \approx 10^3$. These findings indicate that $\eta_{crit}$ can be substantially reduced by increasing solid shear stress or liquid slip. Notably, setting $\tau_s=0$ and $b=0$ recovers the classical no-slip condition, which corresponds to the lowest $\eta_{crit}$ value of 116.8 reported in prior work. These insights offer valuable guidance for designing systems with high collection efficiency. Additionally, we provide a concise review of boundary condition modeling for Newtonian fluids on solids, offering deeper theoretical understanding and a framework for future extensions to other fluids and boundaries. This comprehensive approach enhances both the interpretation and applicability of our findings. Furthermore, we derive a general expression for $\eta$ applicable to arbitrary values of Pe, $b$, and $\tau_s$. Using this formulation, we can both recover the findings from Ref. [1] and explore new parameter regimes. Our analysis demonstrates that $\eta_{crit}$ can be orders of magnitude lower than the no-slip value, reaching as low as $\eta_{crit} \approx 10$. These results offer a theoretical basis for the recent experimental observation of $\eta_{crit} \approx 10$ by Ref. [2]. We conclude that solid shear stress and liquid slip length are critical for achieving high-efficiency droplet collection systems. Supporting this, we present a phase diagram mapping $\eta_{crit}$ against $\tau_s$ and $b$, illustrating how these parameters can be optimized to minimize the required droplet rising distance.

This analysis reveals an inverse relationship between these two parameters: while luminosity, velocity dispersion, and maximum rotation speed scale with the Hubble type, the magnitude of these properties per unit disk area shows an inverse trend with distance. This classification is essential for organizing low-energy effective theories of gravity under $SO(N)$ symmetry. Specifically, we address the sub-question of how to categorize these low-energy effective theories using non-linear transformations of fields. In this initial part, we establish a methodology for achieving such a classification and apply it to a subset of relevant local operators featuring a $F(R)$ structure. In the subsequent second part, we will apply this same methodology to graviton and scalar-field-based effective theories. Our approach builds upon the foundational work of Donoghue [1], which first defined a classification scheme for low-energy effective theories based on the principal kinematic frame of $SO(N)$ symmetry. Our methodology introduces several advancements over Donoghue's approach, including: (i) a resolution to an ambiguity present in his scheme; (ii) a demonstration that his approach constitutes only a subset of all possible methods for classifying low-energy effective theories; (iii) an establishment of a criterion for determining whether a given local operator constitutes independent information; and (iv) the development of an algorithm to systematically identify sets of local operators that contain independent information. Our findings indicate that, contrary to the situation in the principal kinematic frame of the Lorentz group, our method yields a finite number of low-energy effective theories for a given spin when utilizing a specific set of local operators, a result that may seem counterintuitive. Furthermore, our work provides a precise definition of what constitutes a "non-linear transformation of fields," a concept that has previously lacked clarity in the literature. Consequently, our results have significant implications for low-energy effective theories, particularly regarding the definition and identification of new degrees of freedom. Finally, our methodology offers valuable insights into the general structure of local operators found in various low-energy effective theories. This publication [2] will detail the application of this methodology to graviton-based effective theories, while a third publication will extend these results to effectively massless theories of spin-1 and spin-2 particles. Our approach represents a substantial generalization of Donoghue's methodology, which was originally limited to the principal kinematic frame of $SO(3)$. By extending these principles to $SO(N)$, our work provides a framework applicable to a broader range of scenarios. This model represents a novel approach to learning compact, interpretable, and reversible representations of non-stationary data, specifically within the context of stochastic dynamical systems. We demonstrate the application of our PAE to a two-layer Hopfield network, illustrating its efficacy in capturing both the system's marginal distributions and its full joint distribution across spatiotemporal dimensions. Complex systems frequently exhibit high-dimensional dynamics characterized by strong spatiotemporal correlations. Model-free machine learning techniques have proven effective at uncovering hidden low-dimensional structures within such systems; however, these methods typically yield black-box models that lack physical interpretability. In contrast, we introduce a physically-parameterized Probabilistic Autoencoder (PAE) capable of learning reversible models of high-dimensional stochastic dynamical systems. This framework learns two distinct sets of parameters: those governing the system's marginal distribution and those describing the evolution of states over time. We apply this PAE model to a two-layer Hopfield network, a canonical high-dimensional memory system. Our modeling results reveal that the PAE successfully captures the model's time correlations, marginal and joint distributions, and the exchange of information between layers during memory storage. Crucially, by analyzing the physically-parameterized PAE, we gain deep insights into the model's performance, such as how network parameters affect the storage capacity of high-dimensional patterns and the distribution of time correlations during spontaneous pattern retrieval. By connecting the model's physical parameters to its statistical properties, our work provides a new perspective on complex systems that extends beyond the purely statistical description offered by previous model-free methods.

This paper introduces an optimized data structure for marking all reachable markings in Petri nets, designed to accelerate the Marking Reachability Algorithm (MRA). This enhancement substantially improves the efficiency of the BFS component within the MC4C procedure, a key step in constraint-based model checking. Model checking stands as a fundamental technique for analyzing distributed and concurrent systems. Significant efforts have been devoted to optimizing its application for Petri nets, a popular formalism for representing such systems. This article presents an improved algorithm for determining the set of all reachable markings in a general Petri net, known as the Marking Reachability Algorithm (MRA). Given a petri net with $p$ places, $t$ transitions, and an initial marking comprising $k$ tokens, the algorithm operates with a time complexity of $O(tpk^2)$ and a space complexity of $O(tpk)$. Our approach offers an exponential improvement in time complexity over the method by Jeng et al. (1995) and a linear improvement over the approach by Li and Li (2017). Furthermore, we demonstrate that, for a specific class of petri nets, the problem of deciding whether all places are reachable is complete for NP. This finding establishes a lower bound for MRA's time complexity, indicating that further significant optimizations are unlikely. Finally, we examine the parameterizability of MRA; while the algorithm cannot be parameterized by the number of places to achieve better complexity, it can be parameterized by the number of transitions to simplify its structure.

Over the past ten years, rapid progress in quantum computing has been achieved by harnessing rapidly dephasing transmon qubits \cite{Koch2007, Burch2009, Martinis:2005}. These devices consist of Josephson junction circuits exhibiting non-linear inductance, where superconducting tunneling across Josephson junctions enables quantum behavior. Their significant advantages include long coherence times, fast gate speeds, and the ability to read out qubit states via microwave transmission \cite{Murch:2013}. As a result, they have become the leading technology for implementing large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers \cite{Fowler:2012, Martinis:2019}.

Despite this rapid advancement, the transmon's short coherence times remain a barrier to scalability. To reach the fault-tolerant threshold, researchers must improve transmon performance by at least an order of magnitude. This improvement requires a detailed understanding of transmon physics, specifically the relative importance of various loss sources.

Federated learning facilitates model training on data held across multiple devices, making it ideal for Internet of Things (IoT) environments. We introduce the concept of a Tauris bundle as the bundle counterpart to a face of a convex body and define $T$-convexity as the bundle analogue of total nonnegativity relative to a fixed convex body. Our primary objective is to establish fundamental results concerning generalised tropical configurations formed by collections of Tauris bundles. We demonstrate that such configurations give rise to novel geometric objects on projective varieties, specifically asymptotically polyconvex bodies and discrete measures with associated Aubry sets. These constructs serve as the bundle analogues of collective Aubry sets and disintegration measures for collections of tropical configurations. We further examine the projective limit of these structures and link them to established results in both Aubry-Mather and Mañé theories. Finally, we illustrate these concepts and definitions using various examples, including those drawn from Fano varieties. Additionally, we provide a projective bundle characterization of Mañé's nondegenerate collections of convex bodies and derive new findings for the corresponding projective limit. These outcomes rely partly on recent advancements by the third author and S. Kim regarding Mañé theories. Overall, this paper represents an initial attempt to unify both Aubry-Mather and Mañé theories through the framework of Tauris bundles. We anticipate that these methods and perspectives will prove valuable for tackling open problems within this domain. Additionally, we establish a fresh projective characterization of nondegenerate collections of tropically convex sets and novel findings for their associated geometric entities. These conclusions will be detailed in a subsequent publication. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the theory of Tauris bundles offers a natural framework for Mañé duality. ptune exoplanets have revealed a "photoevaporation desert" characterized by a lack of planets with high masses and close-to-star orbits. This study investigates the evolutionary tracks of planets with initial radii between 1.5 and 4 Earth radii, initial orbital periods ranging from 2 to 100 days, and initial masses from 0.5 to 10 Earth masses. We evolved these tracks using a grid of 1D hydrodynamic models to account for the complete transition from XUV-driven to stellar wind-driven atmospheric mass loss. Our results indicate that all tracks begin with rapid XUV-driven mass loss, transitioning to wind-driven loss once the atmosphere contracts sufficiently for the energy-limited approximation to no longer apply. These evolutionary tracks display distinct "knees" marking the shift between wind regimes, revealing a complex "wind-driven desert" in the mass-period-radius parameter space. Furthermore, we find that initial planet mass is a critical factor in determining final states, with more massive planets retaining more atmospheres and surviving longer in the XUV regime. While initial conditions are vital, we also observe that a significant fraction of tracks cross the boundary where planets become observable as rocky cores with radii under 1.5 Earth radii. Finally, we demonstrate that the extended contraction phase of these tracks can be accurately modeled using a simple power-law mass loss formula. These findings suggest that power-law approximations are suitable for simple analytic or semi-analytic studies of atmospheric evolution, and that the observed deserts may result from a combination of atmospheric mass loss and the continued contraction of surviving planets. This study underscores the need for more precise measurements of the initial properties of small exoplanets to better constrain their evolutionary histories. (Abridged)

While prior studies indicate that introducing non-determinism into the actor enhances exploration, it compromises convergence speed and sample efficiency. This study demonstrates the implementation of deterministic policy gradient (DPG) within the actor-critic framework for deep RL. Although DPG is a fully deterministic algorithm, our experiments reveal that it exhibits a degree of non-determinism when integrated with the actor-critic FDDPG. This novel approach was tested on continuous control tasks using MUDDPG, a deep RL algorithm built upon the SUDDPG foundation. Compared to FDDPG, MUDDPG demonstrates superior performance in solving tasks, particularly regarding convergence speed and sample efficiency. Furthermore, we establish that DPG remains effective for a wide range of motor skill learning problems. These findings underscore the continued relevance of deterministic policy gradient methods and highlight the potential for future research into optimizing their hyperparameters. Additionally, we argue for a more balanced investigation into the non-determinism of actor networks, noting that existing literature often overlooks this aspect by focusing predominantly on deterministic actors. Our results suggest that non-deterministic actors do not universally guarantee better exploration, and this point requires further clarification. Empirical evidence supports the use of deterministic policies in specific scenarios, such as solving difficult tasks or when sufficient training data is available. We also provide a theoretical explanation for why DPG achieves effective convergence in actor-critic settings despite its asymptotic non-asymptotic convergence properties. The primary contribution of this work is the demonstration of DPG's success in actor-critic deep RL, even though it asymptotically converges to the wrong solution. This is possible because the actor-critic algorithm operates as an off-policy method, allowing the use of data collected from states slightly distinct from the current policy. Finally, we propose that future efforts should explore novel approaches to deterministically learn Q-functions, a current area of limited research. $p \geq 5$ can be expressed as either $6k \pm 1$ for some integer $k$. While this observation is straightforward, it often sparks curiosity about whether similar patterns exist for primes defined by specific quadratic forms, such as $8k \pm 1$ or $12k \pm 1$. However, a more rigorous framework is necessary to formalize these inquiries. Dirichlet's Theorem on arithmetic progressions guarantees that if $d$ does not satisfy any non-trivial congruence conditions other than those modulo $d$, then there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p \equiv r \pmod{d}$ for any fixed $r$ with $\gcd(r, d) = 1$. This provides definitive answers to questions like the existence of infinitely many primes of the form $8k+1$ or $8k+3$. Conversely, the formula $6k \pm 1$ reflects the fact that $6k$, $6k+2$, and $6k+3$ are all composite; thus, the set of allowable residues modulo $6$ is restricted to $\{1, 5\}$. This leads to the fundamental question: how can one determine the complete list of permissible residues modulo $d$? The solution lies in the theory of quadratic reciprocity and character sums, which definitively resolve this problem. Specifically, one can define a Dirichlet character modulo $d$, denoted $\chi$, and investigate the distribution of primes $p$ where $\chi(p) = 1$ versus $\chi(p) = -1$. The character $\chi$ fully encodes the set of admissible residues. Furthermore, the relative frequency of primes satisfying $\chi(p) = 1$ compared to those with $\chi(p) = -1$ can be determined through these advanced methods. In contrast, the relative counts of primes of the form $8k+1$ and $8k+3$, as well as $8k+3$ and $8k+5$, can be directly inferred from the properties of quadratic reciprocity and the behavior of character sums. Consequently, these techniques not only clarify the frequency of primes in forms like $8k+3$ and $8k+5$ but also provide the deeper theoretical foundation required to address cases such as $6k \pm 1$. lines, was proposed by Witting in 1935 as a complex counterpart to the real configuration of 28 lines discovered by Schläfli in 1850. While the complex lines in this configuration intersect at 120 points and contain 480 intersection multiplicity six curves, a significant distinction from the real lines is that they are not collinear. This paper presents an alternative construction of the Witting configuration using the complex points of Plücker's conic complex, which also encompasses the 480 curves of degree six. Furthermore, we offer an efficient method for generating these curves, highlighting their role as critical components in the theory of algebraic integrable systems. Specifically, these curves are essential for the exact computation of solutions to nonisotropic Lotka-Volterra equations and nonisotropic differential polynomial equations. Additionally, we provide an alternative proof for the simplicity of the groups $S_9$, $S_{16}$, and $S_{17}$, thereby confirming the simplicity of $S_{32}$, and we establish the collinearity of 30 curves of degree six. This dispersion arises from a long-range interaction between the excited state and the condensed ground state, a phenomenon supported by path integral simulations. Furthermore, we reveal that these long-range correlations can originate from a specific class of zero modes, which we define and characterize. Finally, we investigate the connection between these zero modes and the dispersion of charged excitations within the model. These findings suggest that long-range interactions can cause the expected Bogoliubov dispersion in systems with a superconducting gap, a critical factor for the kinetic stability of exotic states like anyons. Additionally, our results indicate that such interactions may emerge in higher-dimensional systems, with potential relevance to highly excited states in superconducting Ising models on hyperbolic lattices. These insights offer a framework for predicting long-range correlations in other topological superconducting systems. Furthermore, we propose a method to construct dispersion for anyons in higher dimensions, a capability essential for the dynamical stability of topological order. This work provides compelling arguments for the stability of anyonic excitations in higher dimensions and establishes a pathway to achieve long-range interactions among anyons. These outcomes are pivotal for the kinematic realization of higher-form gauge theories and higher-rank higher-form anyons. Finally, we demonstrate that the superconducting Ising model can be mapped to a quantum Ising model featuring long-range anisotropic interactions. This model can be simulated using cold atoms on an optical lattice, even when the lattice structure approximates a hyperbolic geometry. This offers a pathway to experimentally observe expected excitations in various topological superconducting phases. Our work also elucidates the role of geometry in topological phases of matter. By examining a model with long-range interactions on a hyperbolic graph, we show that long-range connected states can exist in higher dimensions, a necessary condition for the dynamical stability of topological order. This finding addresses a significant gap in current understanding regarding long-range anyons in higher dimensions. Moreover, our results establish a novel class of long-range connected states in higher dimensions, a discovery that is essential for the dynamical stability of topological order and highly relevant to various experimental systems

A primary analytical goal for such data is identifying species groups that share similar presence patterns. Traditional approaches typically rely on clustering species based on pairwise correlations or similarities, a process that is highly sensitive to data sparsity. Clustering is difficult because the data lacks a natural metric, the high dimensionality often exceeds the number of observations, and the presence is binary.

In contrast, this study proposes a novel method that avoids correlation calculations. Instead, it utilizes a nonparametric Bayesian model that explicitly accounts for data sparsity and multidimensionality. The approach treats species groups as latent variables assigned to each species, with group identities determined by minimizing a penalty for label switching within a group-specific Dirichlet process prior. Species similarities are evaluated by examining the co-occurrence of their group labels across observations.

We assess the method's performance through a simulation study and apply it to an ecological dataset comprising 38 species observed across 1,023 sites within the Amazonian rainforest.

**Keywords:** Dirichlet process, group structure, clustering, presence-absence data, Amazonian rainforest.

This paper investigates the greatest possible value of the sum of the divisors of a non-palindromic number N, denoted as T*, and examines the specific values of N that achieve this maximum. We establish an asymptotic formula for T* and for the set of these maximal numbers, which are characterized as the sum of the divisors of a highly composite number multiplied by the sum of the divisors of a palindromic number. Furthermore, we refine the error term associated with the count of such maximal numbers, drawing a comparison to highly composite numbers. Finally, we present a conjecture regarding the limit of T* divided by N as N approaches infinity. These findings build upon and extend previous research by S. Sándor and others found in references [1] through [6]. Additionally, a computer-assisted verification covers the range from 2 to 10^7. Our computational results indicate that the largest such number N within the range 2 to 10^7 is N = 9999824, yielding a divisor sum of T* = 19999656. However, many OOP purists consider procedural programming to be obsolete, flawed, and inferior. This paper aims to challenge that specific viewpoint.

We argue that procedural programming offers several key benefits, including simplicity, high-level support for abstraction and modularity, and the capacity to facilitate large-scale program development. Additionally, we contend that procedural programming promotes code reusability through the use of functional methods.

Our primary thesis is that procedures serve as a more effective mechanism for large-scale program structuring than methods. We back this claim by presenting a comparative analysis of the C and Smalltalk environments. Finally, our conclusions suggest that procedural programming remains relevant and that procedures and functional methods are invaluable, particularly for structuring and organizing large programs. Consequently, we recommend utilizing C++ or Java to leverage the object-oriented features of these languages.

Supersolid Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) display simultaneous density modulation and spin density modulation in their one-dimensional stripe phase. In this study, we employ a Thomas-Fermot mean field approach to analyze the interaction between a moving impurity and the spin-density modulation. We find that an impurity moving faster than the spin-density wave speed experiences an attractive force from the spin-density modulation at the impurity's position, causing it to be trapped. Conversely, an impurity moving faster than the density wave speed experiences a repulsive force. These findings align with numerical simulations. We also examine the impact of quantum pressure on impurity trapping and compare our results with those of superfluid He-4. Finally, we discuss the experimental feasibility of observing this impurity trapping phenomenon.

Galactic Center (GC) is home to numerous stars orbiting the supermassive black hole Sgr A*. This study examines the proper motions of 115 massive stars within the central parsec, derived from the Gaia Data Release 2 (Gaia DR2) catalog and the Two Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS). We identify 12 new proper motion candidates and establish the membership of 15 previously known objects. Additionally, we propose a revised proper motion catalog for S-stars A0 through A9. Our results highlight several key findings: (1) We confirm the membership of S2, S62, and S67 to Sgr A*, and suggest that S55, S59, and possibly S65 are also members; (2) We report new proper motion candidates that align with the established mass-luminosity relation, including the first identification of an F-type star (S29) in the region; (3) We determine that S29 and S62 are likely X-ray binaries, with S62 potentially hosting a low-mass companion; (4) We identify S40 as a new candidate for the variable star S-100, and we suggest that S25, S29, and S65 are new candidates for S200; and (5) We find that the proper motions of S25 and S40 are consistent with the hypothesis that S200 and S100 share a common origin. These conclusions are based on an analysis of the stars' proper motions, magnitudes, and colors. We conclude that this work expands the known population of stars near Sgr A* and offers a fresh perspective on the dynamics of the existing sample. The data presented in this study will be valuable for future investigations into the dynamics and evolution of the Sgr A* environment. Data from this study will be submitted to The Astronomical Journal. This research utilizes data from the Gaia DR2 catalog, accessible via https://www.cosmos.esa.int/gaia/, and the Two Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS), available at https://www.astro.ucla.edu/~wright/2MASS/. -ray pulse from a free-electron laser can instantaneously eject all core electrons from a single atom, thereby generating a highly charged ion. This process initiates a rapid electron relaxation cascade, which is characterized through time-resolved photoemission and x-ray absorption measurements. In this work, we utilize time-of-flight photoemission to monitor the removal of core and valence electrons on a 100-as timescale following the absorption of a hard-x-ray pulse by a magnesium ion. The data reveal that the ejection of core electrons triggers a dramatic redistribution of the valence electron density around the impact site, resulting in a massive transient flow of valence electrons into the highly charged region. Concurrently, an intense x-ray absorption edge shift indicates that the valence electrons experience a reduction in their kinetic energy. These findings are interpreted within a framework of core and valence electron dynamics, highlighting the creation of novel, transient electronic structures at the femtosecond level. This mechanism of core-excited electron redistribution is anticipated to be a universal phenomenon for atoms and molecules. The ability to manipulate valence electrons on a 100-as timescale opens new avenues for investigating and controlling ultrafast chemical reactions. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that the valence electron density in core-excited ions can be probed via time-resolved photoemission, providing a method to examine electronic properties in various core-excited systems. Additionally, the study of magnesium ions serves as a proof-of-concept for exploring chemical bonding in highly charged, core-excited ionic systems. Finally, this research underscores the efficacy of time-of-flight photoemission for investigating the ultrafast dynamics of highly charged, core-excited ions. This capability is particularly relevant for examining ionization mechanisms driven by x-ray free-electron lasers. This study examines the impact of velocity correlations and shear-dependent viscosity on the time-dependent decay of free energy in 2D colloidal hard-disk systems. We analyze two scenarios: equilibrium systems undergoing viscous cooling and non-equilibrium systems initialized with non-uniform velocity distributions that evolve toward equilibrium. Our findings indicate that velocity correlation decay, a metric for system elasticity, adheres to a universal scaling law across different model systems regardless of their specific rheological behaviors. In contrast, the decay of non-equilibrium free energy displays distinct behaviors for Newtonian and non-Newtonian liquids. Specifically, a power-law decay is observed in Newtonian fluids, whereas free energy decay in non-Newtonian fluids follows a double exponential law. These theoretical predictions are validated through extensive two-dimensional molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, we explore the connection between free energy decay and velocity correlation decay within Newtonian fluids. These insights could enhance the efficiency of thermodynamic integration methods for calculating Helmholtz free energies in complex liquids. Finally, we extend these concepts to practical applications involving confined conditions and spatially varying external potentials. Extending these findings to 3D non-Newtonian liquids remains a subject for future investigation.

These so-called "split graphs" correspond to the data required for the explicit form of the one-loop kernel mentioned in the abstract of [Mar04]. We demonstrate that, assuming an appropriate definition of weights for edges carrying two vertices, the master formula from [Kont94] remains valid for split graphs. In this context, edges with a propagator can be treated as having a weight of $\frac{1}{k^2-e^2}$, where $k$ is a momentum index and $e$ is an index for an associated Lie-algebra generator. Furthermore, we provide a formula for the one-loop regularization of a split graph that maintains the structure of the one-loop definition proposed by Witten in [Wit87], and we estimate the order of the edges within this regularization framework. These results facilitate a more straightforward verification of the master formula in [Kont94] for a significant class of graphs and support the conjecture that an analogous regularization exists for the full (non-split) graph. Finally, we illustrate the application of these findings by explicitly computing the one-loop regularization for a specific graph representing the interaction between two curvature and one connection term. This graph corresponds to a term in the one-loop vertex describing the interaction of two Yang-Mills fields with gravity. Our result aligns with the expectation that the Lie-algebra indices in the split graph are permuted relative to those in the fully regularized graph, a phenomenon observed in similar contexts, such as the one-loop photon field interaction with a Higgs field in the Standard Model [Mar04]. This suggests that the same mechanism likely governs the one-loop photon-Higgs vertex in the theory defined by [Wit89]. Additionally, we propose a method to compute the weights of edges with two vertices for general one-loop graphs, a task that may be even more significant than the explicit calculation for split graphs. In this approach, edges with two vertices are assigned a weight of $\frac{1}{k^2-e_1-e_2}$, where $e_1$ and $e_2$ are the indices of the two vertices. This formula is particularly suited for verifying the one-loop regularization definition in [Wit87] for a broad class of graphs, as it preserves the structure of the Lie-algebra indices found in the tree-level vertex from [Wit87].

Our methodology involves training three distinct systems on a specific task: one utilizing supervised, one using unsupervised, and one applying self-supervised learning. We then evaluate these trained systems on a different task, assessing them through both quantitative and qualitative metrics. The quantitative analysis ranks representations based on their cluster purity within a target space, while the qualitative analysis examines representations using a "similarity graph" that maps each data point to its nearest neighbors. However, this strategy is inherently flawed because synthesizing realistic blurry-sharp pairs is difficult, and the process inevitably introduces artifacts that degrade both synthetic pair quality and final restoration performance. To address this, we introduce a novel artifact-removal-based deblurring framework. This framework deblurs only sharp images, using in-painted patches to create synthetic blurry pairs; consequently, the deblurring network's training objective is to remove artifacts rather than reconstruct blurry images. Our approach, termed Artifact Removal And In-painting for Deblurring (ARID), offers two key advantages: (1) it eliminates the need to design a mapping between artifact and original images for deblurring, as the two networks operate independently; and (2) it avoids the mapping between blurry and sharp images entirely by generating synthetic pairs through patch patchworking and artifact injection. Experimental results demonstrate that ARID outperforms several other deep deblurring techniques, particularly in low-light conditions. The implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/zhenghaozhang/ARID.

Under hydrostatic pressure, it undergoes two phase transitions: one at 12 K to an antiferromagnetic state and another at 23 K back to the paramagnetic phase. While optical and Raman spectra in the 50–300 meV range show complex spectral shapes with many peaks, analysis of the pressure-dependent evolution of specific modes indicates that the transition at 23 K involves a lifting of degeneracy in an already paramagnetic state, suggesting a second-order nature. The observed pressure-induced evolution of superconductivity in Eu2Ir2O7 mirrors the hydrostatic behavior seen in LaAl2CuO4, a cuprate where superconductivity is also suppressed by magnetic phases. The parallel between these two compounds offers new insights into the relationship between magnetism and superconductivity in transition metal compounds. We present POCO, an automated approach for exploring the configuration space of C/C++ programs. POCO operates in two phases: first, it builds a control-flow graph (CFG) of a target binary using Clang's intermediate representation; second, it performs symbolic execution guided by a model of the program's configurability. This model is derived from a static analysis that constructs a dependency graph linking configuration variables to the points where they influence the CFG. Our evaluation shows that POCO is practical, efficient, and superior to four strong baselines. It identified an average of 2.32 unique configurations per system across 21 real-world C/C++ applications, substantially reducing the time needed to uncover new and unique configurations compared to the baselines. Furthermore, POCO detected 87.5% of the unique configurations found in the test suites of these systems.

However, in the presence of a finite detector threshold, these small energy transfers create coupling-dependent distortions to the expected event rate, known as "threshold effects." This paper demonstrates that for dark matter-nucleus scattering, these threshold effects are so pronounced that the rate law does not follow the standard $v^2$ velocity dependence; instead, it exhibits a distinct $v^4$ behavior at low velocities. Consequently, fitting a conventional $v^2$ law to data from experiments with significant threshold effects yields biased results. To address this, we provide a general formula for the differential rate relative to velocity that is applicable across various dark matter models and detector types. Using this general expression, we analyze recent data from the DAMA/LIBRA dark matter experiment, which remains the only collaboration publishing results on sub-GeV dark matter. Our findings indicate that while threshold effects are indeed critical for DAMA/LIBRA, they do not rule out the simplest spin-dependent sub-GeV dark matter model when compared with other data sets. Finally, we examine the feasibility of interpreting future data with the same level of accuracy. Although next-generation direct-detection experiments will be more sensitive, they will also record significantly more background events, making the precise characterization of threshold effects essential for both excluding simple sub-GeV dark matter models and setting limits on more complex variants. Furthermore, given that the nuclear cross section derived from a $v^4$ rate law differs substantially from that derived from a $v^2$ law, we illustrate how this impacts the cross section limits imposed by DAMA/LIBRA. Our analysis shows that when the $v^4$ nature of the rate is accounted for, the spin-dependent cross section limits for sub-GeV dark matter are relaxed by approximately two orders of magnitude. This represents a significant improvement, enabling the use of nuclear scattering as a complementary probe to direct detection of sub-GeV dark matter. Additionally, we note that the same $v^4$ behavior occurs in the single-photon regime, affecting limits derived from XENON1T and LUXZEPLIN. In both instances, the resulting cross section limits are orders of magnitude better than those obtained by ignoring these threshold effects. This work aims to facilitate the comparison of future sub-GeV dark matter searches that incorporate these effects. HUMBI comprises 108,360 instances featuring a single modal inference task, each paired with natural language questions, human-generated justifications, and a justification card. By offering a challenging dataset with justification cards, HUMBI encourages the development of models capable of handling complex queries, diverse OOD questions, multi-turn interactions, and multi-modal in-context learning. Our approach utilizes a shared architecture trained on both English and multilingual data, enabling knowledge transfer through two strategies: direct cross-lingual transfer and a combined method integrating unsupervised back-translation. Specifically, direct cross-lingual transfer outperforms the combined approach, and it achieves results comparable to those obtained using resources native to the target language. Furthermore, our proposed method surpasses previous state-of-the-art techniques. Finally, we find that combining cross-lingual transfer with pretrained contextualized embeddings further enhances performance. These findings hold across multiple tasks, including text classification and question answering. A key implication is that our approach effectively bridges the resource gap between English and non-English languages. The source code and pretrained models are accessible at https://github.com/amanarora/ML-Cross-Lingual-Transfer-NLP.

In recent years, neural machine translation (NMT) has seen substantial progress driven by attention mechanisms and large-scale neural networks. However, these models often struggle with rare words and expressions, a limitation that has spurred interest in incorporating external knowledge. While prior efforts have mainly focused on bilingual encyclopedias like Wiktionary and Wikipedia, this study examines the use of a universal, language-agnostic knowledge graph, ConceptNet. We developed a system utilizing a sequence-to-sequence architecture with attention mechanisms, enhanced by semantic types and relations from ConceptNet to facilitate better knowledge integration. Experiments on the IWSLT'14 French-to-English and IWSLT'15 German-to-English translation tasks reveal that our approach significantly outperforms a baseline system without external knowledge, as well as a system using only a bilingual dictionary. Although adding features through simple average pooling limited improvements, we observed that combining ConceptNet with BERT embeddings via element-wise addition significantly boosted performance in both tasks. These results validate the effectiveness of our methodology for enhancing NMT systems. We have made our code and models publicly available at https://github.com/kyuhyun-lee/ConceptNet-NMT. This paper has been accepted for presentation at NAACL 2019.

While this leveraged knowledge is frequently assumed to be semantic or structural, we demonstrate that agents can effectively borrow even misleading noise from deceptive related tasks. Although such a task appears similar to the current one to a myopic agent, its trajectory noise actually points in the opposite direction. We provide both analytical proof and experimental validation that this negative transfer occurs in a two-dimensional gridworld. Higgs boson, the primary objective of the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has been to measure its properties. While the particle's mass and production methods have been established, further investigations into rare decays remain crucial. One such decay, $H\to\mu^+\mu^-$, offers significant insight into the Standard Model and potential Beyond Standard Model phenomena. This study presents the most current ATLAS findings on this rare process based on data from 13 TeV proton-proton collisions recorded between 2015 and 2016, yielding an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis detects the $H\to\mu^+\mu^-$ signal with a statistical significance of 5.1 standard deviations. Additionally, the branching ratio for this decay is determined to be ${\rm BR}(H\to\mu^+\mu^-) = (2.2 \pm 0.7) \times 10^{-4}$. These results align with Standard Model predictions, and a comprehensive discussion of the interpretation of these findings is provided. Furthermore, a re-interpretation of the data is conducted in the context of a two-Higgs-doublet model, exploring potential deviations from Standard Model expectations. Finally, a search for a second Higgs boson with a mass of 250 GeV is presented, yielding no significant evidence, which translates to 95% confidence level upper limits on the coupling strengths between the additional scalar and fermions and gauge bosons. These limits are also applicable to models featuring an additional standard-model-like Higgs boson. Additionally, a re-interpretation addresses a $U(1)'$ extension of the Standard Model, constraining the model's Higgs-fermion and Higgs-boson coupling deviations. The study concludes with a search for a pseudoscalar Higgs boson ($A$) in the same final state, where the production of the additional scalar is mediated by the standard-model-like Higgs boson fusion, with sensitivity reaching masses up to 130 GeV. This re-interpretation constrains the mass and coupling of this scalar to the fermions and gauge bosons. The search is also interpreted within a supersymmetric framework, specifically a minimal supersymmetric standard model with non-degenerate higgsinos, to constrain sparticle masses. The paper finally presents a search for charginos decaying to a neutral chargino

We derive a novel non-dense, quasi-periodic activation function and apply it to a standard dilated convolution, creating the quasi-linear residual connection. This innovation allows QPNet to match the convergence speed of linear ResNet while maintaining superior representation capabilities compared to standard convolutions. Nevertheless, CF approaches encounter significant hurdles, including the cold-start problem and data sparsity. To address these issues and enhance prediction precision, this paper introduces a hybrid model integrating Deep Learning (DL) and Collaborative Filtering (CF). The proposed system first employs a Deep Neural Network (DNN) to extract features from raw user and item data, which are subsequently fed into a Matrix Factorization (MF) algorithm for CF. In the realm of wireless communication, Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) systems are essential for achieving high data rates and enhanced reliability. While Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) has proven effective in various domains, its application to MIMO channel estimation remains underexplored. This study proposes a novel hybrid framework combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) for accurate channel estimation. The architecture initially utilizes a CNN to automatically extract features from the training dataset before applying LDA to derive the final channel estimate. The efficacy of this approach is validated through simulations using a MISO system with a single transmit antenna and four receive antennas. Simulation results indicate that the proposed model outperforms three baseline systems—LDA, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and Principal Component Analysis with Latent Dirichlet Allocation (p-LSA)—across both small and large training datasets. Additionally, the proposed system resolves the cold-start challenge associated with traditional machine learning-based MIMO channel

exoplanetary radial velocity signals. This study investigates the impact of spotted stars on velocity measurements for two specific stars: HD 155248 and HD 187019. Observations were conducted using the HARPS spectrograph at La Silla and VLT/RAISE at La Silla over a period of 1.5 years. For HD 155248, we detected 18 H-alpha line profiles, classifying it as moderately active, whereas HD 187019 showed no signs of activity. The high cadence of our monitoring allowed us to characterize the activity timescales of these stars. We performed a radial velocity analysis on HD 155248, correlating the velocity data with the chromospheric activity proxy. Our results reveal a strong correlation between H-alpha variability and radial velocity changes, confirming that activity is the dominant factor masking any planetary signal. Consequently, HD 155248 exhibits a rotational period of 10.3 days with an amplitude of 1.5 m/s, while HD 187019 displays a longer period of 30.5 days with an amplitude of 0.8 m/s. These findings suggest that the observed variations in HD 155248 stem from starspots located on the stellar surface. Furthermore, we developed a method to filter out the most significant activity-induced radial velocity signals, which can be applied to future studies of active stars. Ultimately, HD 155248 and HD 187019 serve as valuable case studies for assessing the risks associated with stellar activity when utilizing precise radial velocity techniques. These active stars can be effectively monitored via ground-based optical and near-infrared spectroscopy, offering an alternative to more expensive facilities like HARPS or ESPRESSO. This approach enables the characterization of the most significant activity signals, thereby facilitating a more accurate determination of the remaining in-system radial velocity amplitude. We conclude that the residual amplitude for HD 155248 is 0.3 m/s, and for HD 187019, it is 0.2 m/s. These residuals represent the maximum potential signals that could be mistaken for exoplanetary radial velocity signatures. Our study demonstrates that ground-based optical and near-infrared spectroscopy is sufficient to characterize the most significant activity variations in active stars, allowing for the removal of their influence on radial velocity data. We extend this approach to address editing scenarios involving multiple constraints, such as specifying target values for certain pixels while others must remain unchanged, or requiring that all pixels adhere to a curve or lie between two curves. Utilizing a statistical model for cluster mass distributions, we derive the modified hydrostatic equilibrium equation, incorporating the effective gravitational acceleration from the Finzi model, to analyze temperature profiles. Our results demonstrate that the effects of this modified gravity produce observable deviations in the temperature distribution within galaxy clusters. Furthermore, these deviations provide potential evidence for the validity of the Finzi gravity framework. As a preliminary investigation, we show that the proposed modification to hydrostatic equilibrium alters the relationship between central temperature and cluster size. We predict that the fining exponent, which governs the power-law behavior of this size-temperature relation, should display a slight decrease of approximately 10% to 20% under the modified gravitational law compared to the $\Lambda$CDM model. These findings offer a potential method for detecting large-scale enhancement in the fining exponent and serve as a basis for future research into the observational signatures of fining within galaxy clusters. This framework extends classical extremal problems, such as the Erdős-Pósa conjecture, to the geometric setting. We introduce a novel technique to transform any extremal problem on cghs into a non-geometric counterpart, thereby allowing the application of existing methods that exploit structural properties of obstructions to derive lower bounds for packing numbers. Utilizing this approach, we resolve the Erdős-Pósa conjecture for cghs with bounded rank, confirming a recent proposal by Micek and Ueckerdt. Additionally, we establish a similar result for the geodesic crossing problem, answering a question posed by Micek and Schaefer. From a broader perspective, our findings indicate that numerous techniques from non-geometric extremal combinatorics can be adapted to geometric contexts with minimal degradation in the resulting bounds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the methods discussed in this work apply to hypergeometric graphs, the more general formulation of cghs employed in current packing-and-forcing research. As a specific application, we determine the asymptotic behavior of the maximum k-fractional T-junction packing number in cghs. This advancement relies on solving the associated fractional hitting set problem and confirms a recent conjecture by Ueckerdt and Wood. The results indicate that for cghs with bounded rank, the maximum k-fractional T-junction packing and covering numbers differ only by a constant factor. This conclusion supports the plausibility of the packing-and-forcing conjecture specifically regarding T-junctions. Finally, we confirm a recent proposition by Ackerman and Fox which applies the transform method to cghs of treewidth three. This finding aids in addressing the packing-and-forcing problem for this specific class of cghs and clarifies the structure of minimal T-junction hitting sets within them.

This work not only surpasses existing performance benchmarks but also deepens the understanding of snake movement mechanics. Finally, the experimental data is utilized to propose an optimized geometric model for future snake-inspired robots. These findings offer critical insights into designing faster snake-inspired locomotion systems. Source code and videos are accessible at https://github.com/robotic-snake. Furthermore, the robotic snake is available for purchase at https://robotic-snake.myshopify.com/.

While snakes and snake-inspired robots have effectively navigated challenging terrains, increasing running speed has remained difficult. The main limitation lies in the absence of a stroke capable of generating adequate ground force to drive the body forward at high speeds. Existing robot control strategies rely on simple waveforms, often ignoring the role of vertical forces in acceleration. This study proposes an optimized control strategy for a robot named RoboSnake, leveraging an end-to-end differentiable model to identify an effective locomotion pattern. Unlike prior methods, this approach explicitly examines how vertical forces influence acceleration. Experiments comparing robots controlled by a simple wave versus the optimized strategy confirm the benefits of accounting for vertical force components. Results show that incorporating these forces allows the robot to run faster and climb steeper inclines. The robotic system, including hardware and software, is open-source and can be acquired at https://robotic-snake.myshopify.com/, providing a valuable benchmark for future snake-inspired locomotion research. Supplementary details regarding the robot and experiments are available at the project website https://robotic-snake.myshopify.com/ and at https://github.com/robotic-snake.
